column2: Having obtained him, all the gods gained victory in battle; victory, wrath and valour arose from Ishvara's brilliance.
Having gained victory through Manyu, and engaging the Daityas, all returned as they had come, protected by Manyu.
Where on the Gautami's bank the gods worshipped Shiva and obtained Manyu and victory, that is called Manyu-tirtha.
The man who with self-control remembers the origin of Manyu gains victory and is never overcome by anyone.
There is no purifier like Manyu-tirtha, great sage, where Shankara himself abides always in the form of Manyu; bathing, giving and remembrance there grant all desires.
On that very holy mountain was a Rakshasa named Parashu, terror of gods and Brahmins, hater of sacrifice, slayer of Brahmins,
roaming the forest at will in many forms, sometimes in a Brahmin's form for a moment, sometimes taking a tiger's form,
sometimes a god's form, sometimes bearing an animal's form, sometimes a woman's form, sometimes a deer's,
sometimes a child's form; so the evildoer roamed. Where lived the learned Brahmin Shakalya, the best of sages,
to him that great sinner Parashu, lowest of Rakshasas, came, to the best of Brahmins, the pure Shakalya, constantly,
but though bent on carrying him off and killing him, the evildoer could not. Once the best of Brahmins, having carefully worshipped the gods,
wished to eat and came there; Parashu, sage, assuming a Brahmin's form, loose-limbed, grey, weak, taking a certain girl, said to Shakalya:

Know me, Brahmin, to be a seeker of food, with this girl; you who have reached the guest-hour have fulfilled your duty, giver of honour.
brahmapuran:163:15	Blessed in this world are those whose guests depart from their house with desires fulfilled; others are dead though living.
brahmapuran:163:16	When seated to eat, what is set aside for oneself — whoever gives it to guests has given the earth.
brahmapuran:163:17	Hearing this, Shakalya said, I give it," and seated that Brahmin Parashu, not knowing him,
and duly honoured him; Shakalya gave food. Taking water in his hand to rinse, Parashu spoke:

The deities follow one come from afar and wearied; when he is satisfied they are satisfied, when not, the reverse.
brahmapuran:163:20	A guest and a slanderer: these two are friends of the world; the slanderer takes away sin, the guest is a passage to heaven.
brahmapuran:163:21	He who looks with contempt on a wearied visitor on the road — at that moment his dharma, fame and fortune perish.
brahmapuran:163:22	Therefore, I, a visitor, weary, ask you, best of Brahmins: if you grant my wish, I shall eat, and not otherwise.
It is given, Shakalya said, "eat," to the Rakshasa. Then Parashu said, "I am the best of Rakshasas.
I am not a Brahmin, your enemy, nor old, grey or thin; many years have passed while I have been watching you.
My limbs dry up like a little water in summer; therefore I shall not take you away, I shall eat you with your followers, best of Brahmins."
Hearing Parashu's words, Shakalya spoke:

Those born of great families, who know all scriptures, keep what they have promised; never is it otherwise.
brahmapuran:163:28	Do as is fitting, friend; yet hear my words: the best should speak what is beneficial even to those who are ready to kill.
brahmapuran:163:29	I am a Brahmin, with a body of adamant; Hari protects on every side. May Vishnu guard my feet, the god Janardana my head,
brahmapuran:163:30	may Varaha guard my arms, the king of tortoises my back, may Krishna guard my heart, and Mriga my fingers.
brahmapuran:163:31	May the lord of speech guard my face, may the bird-rider guard my eyes, may the lord of wealth guard my ears, may Bhava guard me everywhere; in manifold calamities, the one refuge is the god Narayana himself.
Having said so, Shakalya said: "Take me or eat me comfortably, Rakshasa-king Parashu; now be unwearied."
At his word the Rakshasa was ready to eat; surely there is not a grain of compassion in the heart of sinners.
With a face terrible with fangs he went near him; seeing that Brahmin, Parashu spoke thus:

I see you, best of Brahmins, with conch, discus and mace in hand, the lord with a thousand feet, heads, eyes and hands,
brahmapuran:163:36	the one abode of all beings, whose form is the Vedic metres, consisting of the world. Today I see you, Brahmin; your former body is no more.
brahmapuran:163:37	Therefore I propitiate you, Brahmin; be my refuge. Give me knowledge, greatly wise one; tell me the holy place that atones for sin.
brahmapuran:163:38	The sight of the great, Brahmin, is never fruitless, whether from hatred, ignorance, chance or negligence.
brahmapuran:163:39	Contact with a touchstone turns iron into gold.
Hearing these words spoken by the Rakshasa, Shakalya, out of compassion, spoke; that Sarasvati is the boon-giver:

Soon, king of Daityas, praise Janardana; for obtaining the fruit of desires there is nothing but praise of Narayana.
brahmapuran:163:42	Hear, Rakshasa, whatever cause there is in this world: that goddess will be pleased with you by my word.
Saying "So be it," Parashu bathed in the Ganga, purifier of the three worlds, and, pure and self-controlled, stood facing the Ganga.
There he saw Sarasvati, of divine form, anointed with divine perfumes, nurse of the world, standing at Shakalya's word,
remover of the world's dullness, mother of the universe, queen of the world; humble-minded Parashu, free of sin, said to her:
The teacher Shakalya said, 'Praise the banner-less husband of Ma (Lakshmi); by your grace let that power be mine.'
Sri Sarasvati said to Parashu, "So be it." By Sarasvati's grace Parashu praised that Janardana
with various words; then Hari was pleased and Janardana, ocean of compassion, gave the Rakshasa a boon:
Whatever the Rakshasa desires in mind, all that will be.
By Shakalya's favour, the Gautami's favour, Sarasvati's favour and Narasimha's favour,
the Rakshasa Parashu, though most sinful, went to heaven, by the grace of the lotus-foot of all holy places, the bow-bearer.
From then on that holy place is known as Sarasvata; by bathing and giving there one is honoured in Vishnu's world.
On that White Mountain many holy places arose from Vag, Java, Vaishnava, Shakalya and Parashu.
With a great army, with his priest, he went to the forest and delighted with charming women, in dance, music and pleasures.
Thus the bow-in-hand king, surrounded by hunters, wandering, once, wearied, came to a tree,
born on the bank of the Gautami, thronged with many flocks of birds, served as if the householder of hermitages, a knower of dharma.
Resting at that best of trees, Pavamana, best of kings, surrounded by people, looked at the excellent tree.
There he saw a stout Brahmin bird with two mouths, of fine form, and, seeing him anxious and weary, the best of kings asked:
Who are you, two-faced bird, who seem full of worry? There is nobody here distressed; why have you come to grief?
Then the bird Chiccika, with mind reassured, slowly, sighing repeatedly, said to King Pavamana:

There is no fear from me for others, nor from others for me; this mountain, strewn with many flowers and fruits and served by sages,
brahmapuran:164:16	I see empty; hence I grieve for myself. I find no happiness, am never satisfied, and nowhere get sleep, rest or peace.
Hearing the two-faced Brahmin's words the king was greatly amazed.

Who are you? What sin was done? Why is the mountain empty? Creatures here on this best of mountains are satisfied with a single mouth.
brahmapuran:164:19	How then will you, with two mouths, not reach satisfaction? Or what wrongdoing did you incur in this birth or before?
brahmapuran:164:20	Tell me all that truly; I shall save you from great fear.
The Brahmin Chiccika, sighing, said to the king:

I shall tell you my former history, Pavamana; hear it. I was a foremost twice-born, versed in the Vedas and Vedangas,
brahmapuran:164:23	of good family, learned, wise, but a spoiler of work, fond of quarrel; I spoke one way in front and another behind, differently to different beings.
brahmapuran:164:24	Always pained at others' prosperity, a deceiver of the world by illusion, ungrateful, devoid of truth, skilled in blaming others,
brahmapuran:164:25	a betrayer of friends, masters and teachers, hypocritical in conduct, exceedingly pitiless, I tormented many people by mind, deed and word.
brahmapuran:164:26	This was my constant amusement: harming others, splitting couples, destroying groups and breaking boundaries.
brahmapuran:164:27	I did this without reflection, averse to serving the learned; there was no sinner like me in the three worlds.
brahmapuran:164:28	Hence I became two-faced, a sharer in sorrow because of tormenting others; and tormented by that sorrow this mountain of mine is empty.
brahmapuran:164:29	And hear another word, king, joined with dharma and wealth: a sin equal to Brahmin-slaying is incurred without it.
brahmapuran:164:30	A Kshatriya who goes to battle, or elsewhere than battle, and kills one fleeing, who has laid down weapons, trusting, turned away,
brahmapuran:164:31	unknown, seated, saying 'I am afraid' — if a Kshatriya kills him, he becomes a slayer of a Brahmin.
brahmapuran:164:32	One who forgets what he has studied, and does excellent work, and shows disrespect to teachers — they call him a Brahmin-slayer.
brahmapuran:164:33	One who speaks kindly to one's face and harshly behind one's back, who always has one thing in heart, another in speech and another in deed,
brahmapuran:164:34	who swears by teachers, who hates, who reviles Brahmins, who is falsely modest, the evil-souled — he is a Brahmin-slayer.
brahmapuran:164:35	One who out of hatred reviles the gods, the Veda, the Self, dharma and the company of Brahmins — he is a Brahmin-slayer.
brahmapuran:164:36	Being such, king, for the sake of show and from shame I behave as if virtuous; therefore, king, I became a Brahmin.
brahmapuran:164:37	Being such, I did some good act somewhere; by that act, king, I myself remember what was done before.
Hearing Chiccika's words, Pavamana, greatly astonished, said to the Brahmin: "By what act is liberation for you?"
Hearing his words, the king of birds said to the king:

On this very best of mountains, on the north bank of the Gautami, is a holy place named Gadadhara; take me there, good vow-holder.
brahmapuran:164:41	That holy place is most meritorious, destroys all sins and grants all desires, so I have heard from great sages.
brahmapuran:164:42	There is nothing else like the Gautami or Vishnu for destroying affliction; may I see that holy place in all respects — this is my wish.
brahmapuran:164:43	By my own effort this can never be done; how can attainment of a desired goal be for those of wicked deeds?
brahmapuran:164:44	Though making effort, hero, I do not see it, it being very hard; so by your favour may I see Gadadhara,
brahmapuran:164:45	who knows grief unasked, ocean of compassion, on seeing whom the afflictions of worldly existence are seen no more by men.
brahmapuran:164:46	Just by seeing him I shall go to heaven, by your grace, good vow-holder.
Thus addressed by the Brahmin Chiccika, the king showed that god and that Ganga to the Brahmin.
Then Chiccika bathed in the Ganga, purifier of the three worlds,

Ganga Gautami, as long as a man does not see you, purifier of the three worlds, he is called a sinner here and hereafter.
brahmapuran:164:50	So lift me, though guilty of all sins, best of rivers; for embodied beings in worldly existence there is no other goal anywhere without you, born from the lotus-feet of Vishnu.
Thus, his soul purified by faith, the Brahmin, with the Ganga as sole refuge, bathed, remembering inwardly, "Ganga, save me."
Then, having bowed to Gadadhara in the sight of the mountain-dwellers, permitted by Pavamana, he at once ascended to heaven.
Pavamana then went to his own city with his followers; from then on that holy place with Chiccika is called Pavamana.
The knowers of the Vedas know it as Gadadhara Kotitirtha; action done there by men becomes ten million times ten million as meritorious.

What is done is to be known as done; what is given to them is imperishable; what is given to those maidens leads to endlessness.
brahmapuran:165:17	Who does not enjoy happiness through sons and grandsons, Sun? One who does it for maidens becomes a vessel of prosperity.
To that maiden Vishti, speaking thus, Bhaskara said:

What shall I do? No one takes you, of terrible form. Family, beauty, age, wealth, learning, conduct, good character —
brahmapuran:165:20	these are looked at mutually in a connection, in marriage, among women and men. We have everything but your good qualities, auspicious one. What shall I do, to whom give you? Why do you reproach me in vain?
Having said so, Bhaskara again said to that Vishti:
If you consent to be given to whoever, I give you today, Vishti; then give me leave.
Vishti said to her father: "Husband, sons, wealth, happiness, long life, beauty and affection arise following earlier deeds.
The action done earlier by a creature, good or bad, produces its fruit accordingly even in another birth.
The father should carefully avoid his own fault; the fruit will be just as the conduct was formerly.
Therefore the father makes the gift-connection suited to his own line; the rest, whatever is to be by fate, will be."
Hearing the daughter's words, the Sun gave that terrifying Vishti, terror of the worlds, to Tvashtri's son Vishvarupa.
Vishvarupa too was likewise terrible, of terrible form. Thus those two roaming together, alike in nature and form,
had sometimes love and sometimes discord between the couple. Sons were born: Ganda and Atiganda,
Raktaksha, Krodhana, Vyaya and Durmukha. The youngest of them was Harshana, meritorious,
a son of good character, fortunate, peaceful, pure-minded, pure. Once he went to see his maternal uncle, Yama's house.
He saw many creatures, some like those in heaven and some suffering; he bowed to his uncle, eternal Dharma, and asked:
Who are these happy ones, uncle, and who are those cooked in hell?
Thus asked, Dharmaraja told everything as it is, and reported the whole course of their actions fully:

Those who never transgress what is prescribed never see hell, those people.
brahmapuran:165:36	Those who do not honour scripture, conduct or the very learned, and who commit transgression of the prescribed, go to hell.
Hearing Dharma's words, Harshana spoke again:

My father is the son of Tvashtri, Bhishana, and my mother is the terrible Vishti, and my brothers are great-souled, and by it they may have peaceful minds,
brahmapuran:165:39	be handsome, faultless and bringers of auspiciousness. Tell me that act today, best of gods; I shall do it,
brahmapuran:165:40	otherwise I shall not go to them. Thus told, Dharmaraja said to the pure-minded Harshana: "You are Harshana, no doubt.
Some sons may be many; they are not threads of the family. Only one son, someone, by whom the family is upheld,
the support of the family, who pleases his parents and lifts his forefathers, he is a son; the others are mere disease.
Because you have said to me, your maternal grandfather's... what is dear, go to the Gautami, bathe with a controlled mind,
and praise Vishnu, source of the world, the peaceful, with a loving heart; if he is pleased he will give all that is desired."
Hearing Dharma's words Harshana went to the Gautami, pure; he praised the lord of the gods, and Hari was pleased.
Then Hari gave Harshana the family's welfare: "May there be welfare for you, preceded by the quieting of all misfortune."
Therefore Vishti is called Bhadra, and the father Bhadra and the sons; from then on that holy place is called Bhadra-tirtha.
Hari, lord of Bhadra, there grants all welfare to men; to men who serve that holy place he gives all success; Janardana, the god of gods, himself is the one treasure of auspiciousness.
Meanwhile Aruna, overcome by sorrow, spoke to the Sun; seeing those two fallen on the ground, Aruna said to the Sun: "Comfort these two, sharp-rayed one, before they die."
Saying "So be it," the Day-maker revived the two birds; Garuda too, hearing of their state, with Vishnu,
came and comforted them and gave them happiness, Narada. Then all went to the Ganga to relieve the burning.
Jatayu and Aruna, Sampati and Garuda, the Sun and Vishnu went to that holy place of much merit.
It is called Patatri-tirtha, destroyer of poison, granting all desires; the Sun himself and Vishnu, with Suparna and Aruna,
and likewise the bull-bannered Lord abide on the Gautami's bank; that holy place is the best of those where the three gods stay.
Having bathed there and become pure, one should bow to these gods; freed from mental and bodily ills, one obtains supreme happiness.
His father diligently (arranged) for his marriage a bed-seat; in the meantime at night, that Brahmin's son lay asleep,
without remembrance of Vishnu, his head gentle, inattentive, on the seat; a cruel-formed Rakshasi, assuming forms at will,
taking him, quickly came to the south bank of the Gautami, on the northern shore of Shrigiri, served by many Brahmins,
a city that was the abode of dharma and of Lakshmi. There the king Brihatkirti, endowed with all Kshatriya virtues,
of immeasurable welfare and plenty — at the night's end that Rakshasi with the Brahmin's son approached that city, ever bearing charming forms.
She roams this entire earth in forms at will; with that Brahmin on the south bank region of the Godavari, the terrible one in the form of an old woman spoke to the Brahmin:

This, best of Brahmins, is the Ganga; let the twilight worship be done together with the best Brahmins; but the best Brahmins at the proper time do not carefully perform the twilight worship —
brahmapuran:167:11	they are called low by the lords of gods, the best among the last-born outcastes. You must say, 'I am your mother'; if not, you will now meet destruction.
brahmapuran:167:12	If you do my word, best of Brahmins, I shall do what is pleasing and happy for you, and bring you again to your country, home and elders; this is truth.
He said, "Who are you?" and the Rakshasi taking forms at will, assuring that confused-minded son of the sage-king with many oaths, said to him:
I am known in the world as Kankalini. The Brahmin too said to her: "What you tell me I shall do, no doubt; whatever is pleasing I say and I do."
